enteric pathogens can grow and survive on the surfaces of plants, and that their survival is affected by the physicochemical properties of the plant surface.

enteric pathogens can survive on plants, but their ability to grow and multiply is limited.

the fitness of enteric pathogens in the plant environment is a complex issue, and the behavior of these pathogens in the plant habitat is influenced by many factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the enteric pathogens have the capacity to survive, multiply, and spread on plants, and the extent of this capacity is determined largely by the plant surface and the environmental conditions under which plants grow and are harvested.

enteric pathogens can grow on fresh produce, and the infectious dose is dependent on the type of produce, the level of contamination, the type of pathogen, the time of exposure to the pathogen, and the physiological state of the pathogen.
the fitness of enteric pathogens in the plant habitat depends on the ability of the pathogen to colonize plant surfaces and the ability of the plants to support pathogen survival and growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that

enteric pathogens, including Salmonella and L. monocytogenes, can survive on plants and that this ability is linked to the ability to form a biofilm, a process that requires the presence of plant exudates and the ability of the bacteria to utilize these exudates.
enteric pathogens can grow and survive on plants, and their fitness is determined by their ability to form biofilms and to compete for nutrients and space with other epiphytic bacteria.

the behavior of enterics in the plant environment is not simply a function of the pathogen's ability to grow on plants, but rather a complex interplay among a number of environmental, microbial, and host factors.
